nodeData.note: Organic IPM, scouting and traps, natural enemies, botanicals, Trichoderma, Pseudomonas and microbial biopesticides.

children.note: Organic integrated pest management builds protection in layers: prevent problems through soil, crop choice and farm design first, then use natural enemies, and only then apply products allowed by organic standards.

Monitoring tells you which pest or disease is present, how much of it there is and whether it is rising. In organic farming it is the step that decides whether any action is needed at all, and which one.
Predators, parasitoids and diseases that attack pests for free. Organic pest control starts by protecting and boosting these allies, then adding releases or introductions where needed.

Pest-control products made from plants: extracts, oils and powders whose natural chemicals repel, deter or kill pests. They break down fast and are usually gentler on people and natural enemies than synthetics, but act more weakly and need correct timing.

Trichoderma is a group of soil fungi used as a biological fungicide. It attacks and crowds out root-rotting fungi and also helps roots grow, so it is mainly used to prevent soil-borne diseases rather than cure them.
Three groups of beneficial bacteria used as biological disease control agents. They protect plants by producing antibiotics, competing for iron and space, and switching on the plant's own defences.

Living fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes that make insect pests and nematodes sick. They act more slowly and more selectively than chemical pesticides and work best as part of integrated pest management (IPM).

nodeData.note: Organic integrated pest management builds protection in layers: prevent problems through soil, crop choice and farm design first, then use natural enemies, and only then apply products allowed by organic standards.

children.note: A way to picture priorities: a wide base of prevention, a middle of biological control and a small tip of allowed products.
Most effort goes into making the farm a poor place for pests and diseases and a good place for crops and natural enemies.

manas.q: What forms the base of the organic IPM pyramid?

children.note: Natural enemies and microbial agents keep pests down once prevention is in place.
Organic-approved sprays are a last resort, used after monitoring shows a threshold has been reached.

manas.q: When should organic-approved sprays be used in IPM?

children.note: Regular scouting decides when to move up the pyramid; see the Scouting, Traps & Thresholds map.
Cultural and physical practices that stop problems before they start.
Balanced nutrition, organic matter and active soil life give vigorous plants and can suppress some soil-borne diseases. Too much nitrogen makes soft growth that aphids and mildews favour.
Choosing varieties with resistance to key local diseases (for example wilt or blight) is the cheapest protection there is.

manas.q: What is usually the cheapest form of crop protection?

children.note: Use certified or carefully selected seed and disease-free seedlings, cuttings and suckers; many viruses, bacteria and nematodes arrive with planting material.
Rotating crop families breaks the life cycles of soil-borne diseases, nematodes and pests that specialise on one family, such as tomatoes, potatoes and peppers.

manas.q: How does crop rotation reduce soil-borne diseases?

children.note: Mixing crops, flowering strips and hedges confuses pests and feeds natural enemies with nectar and shelter.
Trap crops attract pests away from the main crop. In push-pull, desmodium repels stemborers and fall armyworm from maize while border grass attracts them; developed by icipe in East Africa.

manas.q: In push-pull, which plant pushes pests and which pulls?

children.note: Remove and destroy infected plants, fallen fruit (fruit fly) and crop residues that carry disease; clean tools, crates and boots between fields.
Planting early or at a set time can escape peak pest periods; synchronised planting with neighbours shortens the season pests have to build up.
Insect-proof nets, row covers, fruit bags and screened nurseries keep insects out; mulch reduces soil splash that spreads disease.
Covering moist soil with clear plastic for several hot weeks heats the top layer enough to reduce many weed seeds, soil fungi and nematodes.

manas.q: What does soil solarisation use to kill soil pathogens?

children.note: Grafting tomato, eggplant or cucurbits onto rootstocks resistant to bacterial wilt, Fusarium or nematodes protects crops on infested soil.
Drip irrigation, wider spacing and pruning keep leaves dry and air moving, which reduces fungal and bacterial diseases.
Using living organisms to suppress pests and diseases.
Protect existing predators and parasitoids with flowering plants, hedges and by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
Bought predators and parasitoids (for example predatory mites, Trichogramma wasps) are released where natural ones are too few, mainly in greenhouses.
Trichoderma, Bacillus, Beauveria, Metarhizium and viruses such as NPV are used as seed, soil or foliar treatments; see the Biopesticides map.
Biological agents can be killed by copper, sulphur and some botanicals; separate applications in time and check labels.
Products listed by organic standards; always check your certifier's current list and product labels.
Copper hydroxide or oxychloride protects against blights, downy mildews and bacterial spots, but only as a protectant. The EU caps copper at 28 kg per hectare over seven years.

manas.q: What is the EU limit on copper use in organic farming?

children.note: Copper does not break down; it builds up in soil and is toxic to earthworms, soil life and water organisms. A 2024 review argues its risks to non-target organisms are higher than often assumed.
Wettable or dusting sulphur controls powdery mildews and some mites. It can scorch leaves in hot weather and harms predatory mites.

manas.q: Which diseases is sulphur mainly used against?

children.note: A fine white clay sprayed as a particle film that makes leaves and fruit less attractive to insects and reduces sun scorch. It must be washed off produce where residue matters.
A contact fungicide mainly used against powdery mildew; it works best when used early and repeated.

manas.q: What disease is potassium bicarbonate mainly used for?

children.note: Horticultural oils smother soft-bodied insects, mites and eggs and can suppress powdery mildew. Avoid spraying in heat or soon after sulphur.
Potassium salts of fatty acids kill aphids, whiteflies and mites on contact; they need direct coverage and have little residual effect.
Bt toxins kill caterpillars that eat treated leaves; it is safe for most beneficials. Spray young larvae and in the evening, as sunlight breaks it down.

manas.q: Which pests does Bt mainly control?

children.note: A fermentation product of the soil bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa, allowed in many organic standards for thrips, leafminers and caterpillars. It is toxic to bees when wet, so spray in the evening.

manas.q: What organism produces spinosad?

children.note: Neem (azadirachtin) and natural pyrethrins are the main botanical insecticides. Pyrethrins are broad-spectrum and short-lived; neem acts more slowly as an antifeedant and growth regulator.
Garlic, chilli or neem leaf extracts are traditional; strength varies, so test on a few plants first. Certified farms must check whether homemade products are permitted.
Pests can become resistant even to natural products.
Do not use the same product, such as spinosad or Bt, again and again on the same pest; alternate with different modes of action and non-spray methods.

manas.q: How can resistance to spinosad or Bt be delayed?

children.note: Fewer sprays mean less selection for resistance; let thresholds decide.
Under-dosing and poor coverage let partly resistant individuals survive and breed.
Unsprayed areas and natural enemies keep susceptible pests in the population and slow resistance.
Natural products can still be harmful to people, bees and fish.
Wear long sleeves and trousers, chemical-resistant gloves, boots, eye protection and a mask or respirator as the label states. Copper, sulphur and pyrethrins all irritate.

manas.q: Name four items of PPE for spraying.

children.note: Mix outdoors, measure accurately and calibrate the sprayer so the right rate reaches the crop.
Spray in the evening when bees are not foraging, avoid flowering crops and keep a buffer from streams and ponds.
Respect the re-entry and pre-harvest intervals on the label, even for organic products.
Keep products locked, in original containers, away from food and children; rinse containers three times and dispose as advised locally.
Organic standards ban synthetic pesticides; knowing why helps explain the rules.

Synthetic insecticides, fungicides and herbicides (for example organophosphates, pyrethroids, neonicotinoids, glyphosate) are not allowed under IFOAM-based standards, EU, USDA NOP, NPOP (India) or the East African Organic Products Standard.

manas.q: Are synthetic pyrethroids allowed in organic farming?

children.note: They can harm natural enemies, pollinators and soil life, leave residues in food and water, and often trigger pest resurgence and resistance.
Some natural substances are restricted or banned (for example rotenone in the EU, or synergists like piperonyl butoxide with pyrethrins in some standards).
Spray drift from neighbours can break certification; buffer zones, hedges and talking to neighbours help.
In Kenya, biopesticides need PCPB registration and organic produce follows the East African standard; in India, NPOP governs certified export and PGS-India supports local groups.
A written plan pulls the layers together for each crop and season.
List the key pests and diseases of each crop from past records; choose resistant varieties, clean seed, rotation and planting dates.
Prepare healthy soil with compost, use nets or covers on nurseries, sow trap crops or push-pull borders, and apply seed or soil biocontrol.
Scout weekly, keep trap records, and act in order: cultural fixes, biological agents, then allowed products when thresholds are reached.

manas.q: What is the order of actions during the crop in organic IPM?

children.note: Remove residues, record what worked and what did not, and adjust the plan for next season.
A one-page table per crop (pest, prevention, monitoring, threshold, organic action) is enough for most farms and satisfies inspectors.
Videos on organic IPM practices.
eOrganic webinar on building pest management in organic field crops.
icipe explains how push-pull protects maize from fall armyworm.
Access Agriculture shows low-cost natural methods farmers use against fall armyworm.
How to solarise soil with clear plastic to reduce soil-borne pests.
FAO short guide to protective clothing when using pesticides.
Further reading on organic plant protection.
East African guide to organic pest and disease control.
Review of IPM impacts for smallholders in Asia and Africa.
Review of low-cost, smallholder-friendly fall armyworm management.
Regulation renewing copper approval with a 28 kg/ha seven-year cap.

nodeData.note: Monitoring tells you which pest or disease is present, how much of it there is and whether it is rising. In organic farming it is the step that decides whether any action is needed at all, and which one.

children.note: Monitoring turns guessing into decisions: you act only when and where a problem is real.
Most pests and diseases are far easier to manage organically while they are small and patchy; early detection gives time for low-cost measures such as hand picking or removing infected plants.

manas.q: Why is early detection especially important on organic farms?

children.note: Scouting often shows that a pest is below damaging levels or already controlled by natural enemies, so a spray would only cost money and harm beneficials.
Re-scouting a few days after any action shows whether pest numbers really dropped, and builds farm-specific experience for next season.
A routine walk with a fixed pattern, a fixed number of plants and a simple record sheet.
Walk a W or Z shape across the field so that edges and centre are both sampled; avoid only checking the easy rows near the path. Look at plants at several evenly spaced stops.

manas.q: Which walking patterns are used for scouting a field?

children.note: The FAO farmer field school guide for fall armyworm on maize uses five stops along a W walk, checking ten plants at each, so 50 plants per field. Use the method your local extension recommends for other crops.

manas.q: How many maize plants does the FAO fall armyworm scouting method check per field?

children.note: Weekly is a common routine, and more often (twice a week) during sensitive stages such as seedling, flowering and fruit set or when weather favours disease.
Pests often enter from field edges, near weedy borders or neighbouring crops; diseases often start in low, wet or shaded corners. Check these separately as well as the main sample.
Check upper and lower leaf surfaces, growing tips, stems, flowers, fruit and the soil surface; many insects hide under leaves or inside whorls and fruit.
Date, field, crop stage, pest or disease, number of plants checked, number affected (or insects per plant/trap), natural enemies seen, weather and any action taken.

manas.q: Name five things to write down on a scouting record.

children.note: Note ladybirds, lacewings, hoverfly larvae, spiders, parasitised (mummified) aphids and diseased caterpillars. Many natural enemies can mean the pest will be controlled without a spray.
A 10x–20x hand lens and good observation reveal small pests and early symptoms.
A simple 10x–20x lens shows mites, thrips, young aphids, whitefly nymphs, eggs and fungal growth that are hard to see with the naked eye.

manas.q: What magnification of hand lens is useful for scouting?

children.note: Look for chewed holes, windowing, mines in leaves, frass (droppings), sticky honeydew, sooty mould, curled leaves, silvery stippling and webbing.
Look for leaf spots with rings or haloes, wilting with brown stem tissue, powdery or downy growth, cankers, rots and mosaic or mottled leaves.

Nutrient deficiency, herbicide drift, waterlogging, drought and sun scorch can look like disease. A pattern across the whole field or along rows often points to soil, water or spray causes rather than a pest.
Tapping a branch over a white sheet or tray dislodges mites, thrips, beetles and caterpillars so they can be counted.
Bag fresh affected plant parts (with some healthy tissue), label them and take them to a plant clinic or extension office the same day.
Coloured sticky cards catch small flying insects and show when they arrive and how numbers change.
Yellow attracts whiteflies, aphid winged forms, leafminer flies, fungus gnats and some thrips. Widely used in greenhouses and nurseries.

manas.q: Which pests are mainly monitored with yellow sticky traps?

children.note: Blue is especially attractive to thrips, including western flower thrips, so it is often preferred where thrips are the main concern.

manas.q: Which pest group are blue sticky traps mainly used for?

children.note: Hang traps just above the crop canopy and raise them as the crop grows; place some near doors, vents and edges. Follow local guidance for number per area.
Count catches weekly on a marked grid area, record them and replace cards when dusty or full. A rising count is an early warning.
They also catch beneficial insects such as parasitic wasps, so avoid excessive numbers when biological control is used. Trap counts show trends, not exact field populations.
Traps baited with a synthetic copy of a female sex pheromone or other attractant catch mainly males of one species.
The lure releases a species-specific scent that draws males into a trap (funnel, delta or water trap). Because they are specific, they mostly do not catch beneficials.

manas.q: Why do pheromone traps catch few beneficial insects?

children.note: Funnel traps with fall armyworm lure show when moths fly into maize areas. Catches signal the need to scout plants closely; they do not by themselves show crop damage.
Delta or water traps with Tuta lure detect the tomato leafminer very early, even at low numbers, in greenhouses, nurseries and open fields.
Methyl eugenol strongly attracts males of Bactrocera dorsalis (oriental fruit fly) and related species, important pests of mango and other fruit.

manas.q: Which fruit fly is strongly attracted to methyl eugenol?

children.note: Cue-lure attracts males of other species, such as the melon fly (Zeugodacus cucurbitae) in cucurbits. Use the lure that matches the fly species in your crop.

manas.q: Which lure is used for melon fly in cucurbits?

children.note: Protein food baits attract both sexes, especially females looking for protein before egg laying. They complement male lures for fruit fly control.
Change lures as the label states (often every few weeks), store unused lures cool and sealed, handle with gloves and never put two different lures in one trap.
Moth catches show presence and timing; decisions still need plant inspection for eggs, larvae and damage.

manas.q: Can a pheromone trap count alone tell you to spray?

children.note: Other traps for night-flying insects and ground-dwelling animals.
A lamp over a tray or funnel attracts night-flying moths, beetles and leafhoppers. Useful for timing flights of moths such as stem borers, but they catch many non-target insects.
Solar-powered models are used where there is no electricity; switch them on only for monitoring periods to limit harm to beneficial night insects.
A cup sunk level with the soil surface catches ground beetles, spiders, crickets, cutworms and slugs that walk into it. Used to compare ground-dwelling life between fields.

manas.q: What does a pitfall trap catch?

children.note: A sweep net swung through grass or low crops samples active insects; a beat sheet under a shaken branch samples tree and bush pests.
Thresholds turn counts into a decision about whether to act.
The pest level at which the value of crop lost equals the cost of control. Below it, control costs more than it saves.

manas.q: What is the economic injury level?

children.note: A lower level at which you act so that the pest never reaches the injury level. It allows time for the control to work.

manas.q: Why is the action threshold set below the economic injury level?

children.note: They depend on crop, stage, price, cost of control and natural enemies. Use values from local research or extension; where none exist, treat published figures as rough guides.
Some pests need action at first detection: quarantine pests, virus vectors in seed crops and fruit flies in export produce.
For diseases, action is often based on weather (long leaf wetness, humidity, temperature) and first symptoms, since protectant products must go on before infection.
Using attractants not only to monitor but to reduce pest numbers.
Many traps per area remove large numbers of adults. It works best for low-to-moderate populations, in enclosed or isolated sites, and alongside other measures.

Male fruit fly lures combined with a small dose of an approved killing agent on bait stations remove males so fewer females are mated. Check that the killing agent is allowed by your organic certifier.

manas.q: What is the male annihilation technique?

children.note: Dispensers fill the air with pheromone so males cannot find females, reducing mating and next-generation larvae. Widely used against codling moth and other orchard moths.

manas.q: How does mating disruption reduce pest numbers?

children.note: Mating disruption needs large blocks, uniform coverage and low starting pest pressure; small or isolated plots get mated females flying in from outside.
Attract-and-kill combines lure and a killing agent in small spots; the sterile insect technique releases sterile males. Both are area-wide tools usually run by programmes rather than single farms.
Records make monitoring useful over years and are required for organic certification.
Use a fixed form or notebook page per field per visit, with columns for pest, count, plants checked and natural enemies; photos on a phone help.
Plotting weekly trap catches shows the start of flights and peaks, helping time scouting and controls each season.
Organic inspectors ask for records of pest problems, monitoring and every input applied, including product, rate, date and reason.

manas.q: Why do organic farms need written pest records?

children.note: Comparing years shows which fields, varieties and planting dates have fewer problems, guiding rotation and planning.
Digital tools and clinics help diagnose problems, but should be checked against expert advice.
Phone apps such as PlantVillage Nuru and Plantix let farmers photograph a leaf and get a suggested diagnosis using image recognition, sometimes offline.

manas.q: How do phone diagnosis apps identify plant problems?

children.note: Early models scored very high on clean lab images but less well on field photos unlike their training data. Apps can also suggest products not allowed in organic farming; always check.
Photograph in daylight, one leaf or fruit filling the frame, in focus, with both early and advanced symptoms; take several pictures.
CABI PlantwisePlus supports plant clinics where trained plant doctors diagnose samples brought by farmers and give written advice, in many countries including Kenya and India.

manas.q: What happens at a PlantwisePlus plant clinic?

children.note: In Kenya, county extension officers and KALRO; in India, KVKs and state agricultural universities can confirm difficult cases or test samples.
Short videos on scouting, traps and plant clinics.
Access Agriculture shows how to walk a maize field and check plants for fall armyworm.
An introduction for farmers on how to scout vegetables regularly and record what you see.
Utah State University Extension shows what to look for on plants and how to check them.
icipe explains protein food baits for fruit fly management in fruit crops.
GreenhouseIPM shows how sticky traps are used for mass trapping in greenhouses.
CABI PlantwisePlus shows a plant clinic where farmers bring samples for diagnosis.
Further reading on monitoring and thresholds.
FAO guidance on monitoring and managing fall armyworm.
Factsheets and pest management decision guides for farmers and advisers.
East African farmer information on pests, traps and organic control.
Review of how pheromones are used for monitoring, mass trapping and mating disruption.

nodeData.note: Predators, parasitoids and diseases that attack pests for free. Organic pest control starts by protecting and boosting these allies, then adding releases or introductions where needed.

children.note: Key ideas before you start.
Predators eat many prey; parasitoids lay eggs in or on one host which is then killed; pathogens (fungi, bacteria, viruses) make pests sick.

manas.q: What are the three main groups of natural enemies?

children.note: Conservation (protect the enemies already there), augmentation (release more), and classical (introduce an enemy from the pest’s home region).

manas.q: Name the three strategies of biological control.

children.note: Biocontrol aims to keep pests below damaging levels, not to wipe them out — a few pests must remain to feed the enemies.
Smallholder pest management relies heavily on natural enemies; rushing to chemical sprays against fall armyworm risks destroying them.

links.label: 📄 Harrison et al. 2019, J. Environ. Management

children.note: Hunters that eat many prey during their life. Often the larvae eat more than the adults.
Adults and the alligator-shaped larvae eat aphids, scales, mealybugs and mite eggs. Yellow egg clusters stand upright on leaves.

manas.q: What do ladybird larvae look like?

children.note: Green lacewing larvae (“aphid lions”) have sickle jaws and eat aphids, whitefly, thrips and caterpillar eggs. Eggs sit on hair-like stalks.

manas.q: How can you recognise lacewing eggs?

children.note: Adults look like small wasps and hover over flowers; their legless, slug-like larvae eat large numbers of aphids.
Tiny, fast-moving mites (e.g. Phytoseiulus, Amblyseius/Neoseiulus) that eat spider mites and thrips; widely used in greenhouses including Kenya’s flower farms.
General predators present in nearly every field; they catch moths, leafhoppers and flies. Very sensitive to broad-spectrum sprays.
Some ants hunt caterpillars and eggs and help control pests (e.g. weaver ants in mango and citrus), but others protect aphids and mealybugs for their honeydew.

manas.q: Why can ants be both helpful and harmful?

children.note: Night hunters at soil level that eat caterpillars, slug eggs, and fall armyworm larvae hiding in maize whorls.
Insect-eating birds feed on caterpillars; bats eat night-flying moths. Trees, perches and nest boxes keep them around the farm.
Mostly tiny wasps (and some flies) whose larvae develop inside or on a pest and kill it. Usually specialists on a few hosts.
Egg parasitoids kill the pest before it hatches — no damage at all. Larval parasitoids kill later, after some feeding.
Minute wasps that parasitise moth eggs (stem borers, bollworms, fruit borers). Parasitised eggs turn black. Reared on a factitious host and sold as cards.

manas.q: What colour do moth eggs turn when Trichogramma parasitises them?

children.note: Braconid wasps whose larvae grow inside caterpillars, then spin small white cocoons on or beside the host. Cotesia flavipes is used against maize stem borers in Kenya.
In 2018 surveys in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania, Cotesia icipe was the dominant larval parasitoid, parasitising 16–42% of larvae.

manas.q: Which larval parasitoid dominated fall armyworm in East Africa?

children.note: An egg parasitoid of fall armyworm from the Americas, found already present in Africa; in Kenya it parasitised up to 69% of eggs in surveys.

manas.q: Which wasp attacks fall armyworm eggs?

children.note: Encarsia formosa parasitises greenhouse whitefly nymphs, which turn black. A standard greenhouse release worldwide.
Aphidius wasps lay eggs in aphids; the aphid swells into a tan, papery “mummy” with a round exit hole when the wasp leaves.

manas.q: What is an aphid mummy?

children.note: Making the farm a good home for natural enemies. The cheapest and most important strategy.
Synthetic pyrethroids, organophosphates and neonicotinoids kill enemies faster than pests, often causing pest outbreaks afterwards.

manas.q: Why do broad-spectrum sprays often cause pest outbreaks?

children.note: On beans in Tanzania, plant extracts harmed ladybirds and spiders much less than a synthetic pyrethroid.
Some biopesticides cause hidden sub-lethal harm to parasitoids, so spray only when needed and spot-treat.
Strips of flowering plants give adult parasitoids and hoverflies nectar and pollen. A synthesis found flower strips raised pest control in nearby fields by 16% on average.

manas.q: By how much did flower strips raise pest control on average?

children.note: Flower mixes chosen for the target enemies cut cereal leaf beetle damage in wheat by about 61%.

links.label: 📄 Tschumi et al. 2015, Proc. R. Soc. B

children.note: Plants with small open flowers — coriander, dill, fennel, buckwheat, alyssum, marigold, sunflower — feed tiny wasps that cannot reach deep flowers.
Hedges and trees shelter predators, birds and overwintering insects. The synthesis found less clear pest-control gains from hedgerows than from flower strips.
Raised grassy strips across a field where ground beetles and spiders shelter, then move into the crop to hunt.
Mulch, residues and cover crops shelter spiders and ground beetles and keep humidity for insect-killing fungi.
Desmodium intercrop and Napier/Brachiaria border developed by icipe in Kenya reduce stem borer and fall armyworm and support natural enemies.
Adding natural enemies when local numbers are too low or too late.
Inoculative: release a few early so they multiply through the season. Inundative: release large numbers for a quick knock-down.

manas.q: What is the difference between inoculative and inundative release?

children.note: Greenhouses and high-value crops (flowers, vegetables) where conditions are controlled — e.g. predatory mites in Kenyan rose farms.
Buy from registered suppliers; check the batch is alive and fresh, keep cool and out of sun, and release within a day or two.
Cards carry parasitised eggs about to hatch. Staple them under leaves in the crop at the first moth egg-laying; repeat at intervals.
Some enemies (Trichogramma, lacewings) can be reared in simple community labs; India and Pakistan have many such units.
Release in early morning or evening, spread across the field, and stop insecticide sprays before and after release.
In Kenya, KEPHIS and PCPB regulate import and sale of biocontrol agents; in India, the CIB&RC and ICAR-NBAIR guide this.
Bringing a specialist enemy from the pest’s native home to control an invasive pest.
Invasive pests often arrive without their natural enemies. A carefully tested specialist enemy can establish and spread by itself.
Phenacoccus manihoti, from South America, reached Africa in the early 1970s and spread across West and Central Africa, stunting and killing cassava.
A tiny encyrtid wasp (now Anagyrus lopezi) found in the mealybug’s home region of Paraguay and southern Brazil.

manas.q: Which wasp controlled cassava mealybug in Africa?

children.note: After releases from 1981 (some by air) it established in 26 African countries and brought mealybug down to acceptable levels in most fields.

manas.q: In how many African countries did the cassava mealybug wasp establish?

children.note: Hans Rudolf Herren, who led the programme at IITA, received the 1995 World Food Prize for it.
The same wasp was released in Thailand and other South-East Asian countries around 2010 when the mealybug invaded there.
Candidates are tested in quarantine for host range so they do not attack native species; only governments and research bodies should introduce them.
Learn to tell friends from foes before spraying.
A 10× lens shows mites, tiny wasps, aphid mummies and parasitised eggs that are invisible to the naked eye.
Black eggs, bronze or tan aphid mummies, white cocoons on caterpillars, and swollen or sluggish larvae all show parasitoids at work.

manas.q: Name two signs that parasitoids are active.

children.note: Ladybird larvae look like small black lizards and are often killed as pests; hoverfly larvae look like tiny slugs.
When scouting, count enemies as well as pests. Many enemies and rising mummies mean the pest may soon crash without spraying.
Insect zoos and field-school exercises help farmers see predators eat pests — FAO and CABI use them widely in Africa and Asia.
Common errors.
Most insects in a field are harmless or helpful. Spraying everything removes the free control.
Purchased wild-collected ladybirds often fly away; conserving local ones usually works better.
Enemies need time to build up; tolerate some early damage instead of spraying at the first pest.
Videos on natural enemies and biocontrol.
Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT — mealybug and its biological control in cassava.
CABI PlantwisePlus — sustainable management of papaya mealybug in Kenya.
NIPHM (India) — rearing Trichogramma and making release cards.
CABI PlantwisePlus — fighting crop pests with locally reared parasitoids.
eOrganic — how researchers and farmers monitor natural enemies on organic farms.
One Minute Bugs — close-up of a hoverfly larva clearing aphids on cucumber.
Key sources.
Albrecht et al. 2020 — how floral plantings affect pest control and yield.
Neuenschwander 2001 — the story and lessons of the African programme.
Harrison et al. 2019 — low-cost options that protect natural enemies.
Overview of predators, parasitoids, pathogens and strategies.

nodeData.note: Pest-control products made from plants: extracts, oils and powders whose natural chemicals repel, deter or kill pests. They break down fast and are usually gentler on people and natural enemies than synthetics, but act more weakly and need correct timing.

children.note: What botanicals are and where they fit in organic pest management.
Plants make bitter, toxic or smelly compounds (limonoids, pyrethrins, alkaloids, essential oils) to defend themselves. Botanical pesticides borrow these chemicals.

manas.q: Where do the active chemicals in botanical pesticides come from?

children.note: Commercial, registered products with a measured active ingredient (e.g. azadirachtin, pyrethrins), and farm-made extracts whose strength varies from batch to batch.
They are a later step after prevention, monitoring and conserving natural enemies — used to bring a rising pest down, not sprayed on a calendar.
Worldwide, products based on neem (azadirachtin) and pyrethrum remain the main commercial botanicals; plant essential-oil products are newer.

manas.q: Which two botanicals dominate the commercial market?

children.note: Reviews conclude botanicals may help most in tropical developing countries, where source plants grow locally and synthetic products are costly and risky to users.
Most botanicals work in one or more of these ways; few kill as fast as synthetics.
Makes leaves taste bad, so insects stop or reduce feeding and starve slowly. Neem is the classic antifeedant.

manas.q: What does an antifeedant do?

children.note: Strong smells or irritants (garlic, chilli, essential oils) keep pests away or stop egg-laying, but only while the smell lasts.
Azadirachtin disrupts moulting hormones, so young insects fail to moult properly and die or become deformed adults.

manas.q: How does azadirachtin affect young insects?

children.note: Kills insects that are hit directly, e.g. pyrethrins on the nervous system, or soaps and oils that break or block the insect body.
Pyrethrum and soaps act within hours; neem and many plant extracts act over days. Farmers may think a slow product failed when it is working.
Neem tree (Azadirachta indica, Meliaceae), native to South Asia and widely planted in dry tropical Africa including Kenya’s coast and north.
The main active compound, a limonoid found mostly in the seed kernel. Other neem compounds add repellent and antifeedant effects.

manas.q: Which part of the neem tree holds most azadirachtin?

children.note: Dried seeds are de-shelled, kernels pounded, soaked overnight in water, filtered and sprayed, often with a little soap to help it spread.
Pressed from kernels. Works as an oil (smothers soft insects, mite eggs) plus mild azadirachtin effect; needs an emulsifier to mix with water.
The residue after oil pressing, applied to soil. It adds organic nitrogen and helps suppress soil pests and some nematodes.

manas.q: What is neem cake used for?

children.note: Best on young caterpillars, leafminers, whiteflies, aphids, thrips and some mites; weaker on hard-bodied beetles and adult moths.
Azadirachtin degrades quickly in sunlight and heat, so spray late afternoon and repeat after about a week or after rain.
Old, damp or mouldy seed loses azadirachtin and can carry aflatoxin moulds. Use clean seed dried in shade and stored dry.
Dried flowers of Chrysanthemum (Tanacetum) cinerariifolium; the active compounds are called pyrethrins.
Pyrethrins attack the insect nervous system and give quick knockdown. In sub-lethal doses they also repel.

manas.q: How do pyrethrins kill insects?

children.note: In 1998 Kenya grew about 90% of the world’s pyrethrum. Output later collapsed and Tasmania (Australia) is now the main producer.

manas.q: What share of world pyrethrum did Kenya produce in 1998?

children.note: Kenya’s government and the Agriculture and Food Authority are trying to revive the crop in highland counties as a cash crop.
Pyrethrins also kill bees, ladybirds and parasitoids they touch, and are toxic to fish. Spray only infested spots, in the evening.
Breaks down within hours to days in sunlight, so little residue — but also little lasting protection.
Pyrethroids (e.g. permethrin, lambda-cyhalothrin) are synthetic copies. They last longer and are NOT allowed in organic farming.

manas.q: Are pyrethroids allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Many pyrethrum products contain the synthetic synergist piperonyl butoxide (PBO). Most organic standards do not allow PBO — check the label.
Common plants that smallholders in East and southern Africa use as farm-made sprays.
Tephrosia vogelii (fish-bean), a shrubby legume. Leaves contain rotenoids such as deguelin and rotenone; also used as a fallow and green manure.

manas.q: Which toxic compounds does Tephrosia contain?

links.label: 📄 Mkindi et al. 2018, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Rotenoids are highly toxic to fish and moderately to mammals. Rotenone is no longer permitted in EU or US organic standards.
Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower), a common hedge weed. Leaf extract is used against bean pests; the leaves also make an excellent green manure.
On beans, extracts of Tithonia, Tephrosia, Vernonia and Lippia controlled key pests about as well as a pyrethroid, with less harm to ladybirds and spiders.

manas.q: How did plant extracts compare to a pyrethroid on beans in Tanzania?

children.note: Lantana camara, an invasive shrub. Leaf extracts were tested on legumes; using it is fine, but never plant or spread it.

links.label: 📄 Mkindi et al. 2018, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: In lab tests on fall armyworm, Lippia javanica gave high larval mortality and lemongrass was a strong feeding deterrent.
Seeds of Annona squamosa (sitaphal) contain acetogenins that kill sucking pests and caterpillars; used in India. Seeds are poisonous — keep from children and eyes.
Simple farm-made repellent sprays.
Crushed garlic releases sulphur compounds (allicin) that repel aphids and other soft insects; effect is mostly repellent and short-lived.
Hot chilli contains capsaicin, which irritates insects and deters feeding. It also burns human skin and eyes: wear gloves and goggles.

manas.q: What is the active compound in chilli sprays?

children.note: Often added to garlic–chilli mixes for extra smell and irritant compounds; evidence for them alone is limited.
Pound the fresh material, soak in water for a day, strain through cloth, add a little plain soap, dilute and test on a few plants first.
Strong extracts and soap can scorch leaves. Spray a few plants, wait 1–2 days, and look for burnt spots before treating a whole field.
Concentrated oils (e.g. clove, thyme, rosemary, citrus, mint) repel or kill on contact. They evaporate fast and can damage leaves at high doses.
Physical-action products widely used in organic growing.
Potassium salts of fatty acids dissolve the waxy coat of soft insects (aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs, mites) so they dry out. Must hit the pest directly.

manas.q: How does insecticidal soap kill insects?

children.note: Household detergents and washing powders are not the same; many contain additives that burn plants.
Light plant or refined mineral oils coat and suffocate eggs, scales, mites and young insects. Avoid in strong heat or on stressed plants.
Soaps and oils work only while wet, so good coverage, including leaf undersides, matters more than strength.
Tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) sprays are traditional but should be avoided.
Nicotine is absorbed through skin and is poisonous to people and livestock; mixing and spraying tobacco tea causes poisoning.

manas.q: Why is tobacco extract a dangerous pesticide?

children.note: Nicotine is a broad nerve poison that also kills bees, parasitoids and predators.
Tobacco can carry tobacco mosaic virus, which spreads to tomato, pepper and other relatives.
Nicotine and tobacco extracts are prohibited in organic standards (e.g. EU, USDA, East African Organic Products Standard).

manas.q: Is tobacco extract allowed in certified organic farming?

children.note: In lab tests tobacco killed fall armyworm larvae well — effectiveness does not make it safe or organic.
Natural does not mean harmless.
Wear gloves, long sleeves and eye protection; keep extracts away from children; label containers; respect a waiting period before harvest.
Spray in the evening when bees are not flying and avoid open flowers. Azadirachtin has harmed stingless bee queens in lab studies.
Plant extracts usually spare ladybirds and spiders better than synthetics, but some botanicals still reduce parasitoids through sub-lethal effects.

manas.q: Are botanicals completely safe for natural enemies?

links.label: 📄 Mkindi et al. 2018, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Pyrethrum, Tephrosia and tobacco are toxic to fish. Never wash sprayers or dump leftovers in streams or ponds.
Botanicals lose strength fast.
Use the same day or within 1–2 days; they ferment and lose activity. Make only what you will spray.

manas.q: How long do farm-made plant extracts keep?

children.note: Formulated products last longer; store cool, dark and dry, and follow the label expiry date.
Dry leaves and seeds in shade and keep in airy bags; damp storage brings mould and loss of activity.
What research says about botanicals.
Hundreds of plants kill pests in the lab, but few have solid field data; results vary with plant source, season and preparation.
East African trials on bean, cowpea and pigeon pea found yields with the best plant extracts often comparable to a synthetic pyrethroid.

manas.q: Which plants performed best in the East African legume trials?

links.label: 📄 Mkindi et al. 2018, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Active-ingredient content changes with plant age, soil, season and drying, so farm-made sprays are hard to standardise.
Strict registration in Europe and North America has kept the number of commercial botanicals small.
What certified organic farms may use (always check your certifier).
Azadirachtin/neem products, natural pyrethrins (without PBO), potassium soaps, plant and paraffin oils, and approved plant extracts.

manas.q: Name three botanical-type products allowed in organic farming.

children.note: Tobacco/nicotine, rotenone in EU and US standards, synthetic pyrethroids, and any product mixed with synthetic pesticides.
Commercial products need PCPB registration in Kenya and CIB&RC registration in India; farm-made sprays for own use are a separate matter.
Videos on making and using botanicals.
Access Agriculture — step-by-step preparation of neem kernel spray by farmers.
Steven Belmain (Natural Resources Institute) — making and using pesticidal plant sprays in Africa.
Alabama Cooperative Extension — what botanicals are and how to use them safely.
Backyard Farmer (University of Nebraska) — how oils control pests and when not to use them.
Agriculture and Food Authority — growing pyrethrum, Kenya’s “white gold”, again.
Authoritative reviews and references.
Review of where neem, pyrethrum and essential oils stand today.
Field trials in East Africa on yields and beneficial insects.
Review of turning local African pesticidal plant uses into products.

nodeData.note: Trichoderma is a group of soil fungi used as a biological fungicide. It attacks and crowds out root-rotting fungi and also helps roots grow, so it is mainly used to prevent soil-borne diseases rather than cure them.

children.note: A fast-growing, free-living soil fungus found in most soils, especially those rich in organic matter. Colonies turn green as they produce spores.
Trichoderma is a filamentous fungus (mould), not a bacterium. It lives freely in soil and on roots and decaying organic matter, not inside a host plant.

manas.q: Is Trichoderma a bacterium or a fungus?

children.note: One of the earliest and most widely used species in Indian biocontrol products, used for seed treatment and soil application against root rots and wilts.
A very common biocontrol species, valued for strong mycoparasitic activity against soil fungi such as Rhizoctonia and Sclerotium.
A species used in many newer registered products, including in Kenya; it colonises roots well and is used against root rots and wilts.
In culture or on enriched manure it first grows as white threads, then becomes dark green as it sporulates. The green colour is a quick field sign of good growth.

manas.q: What colour does a mature Trichoderma colony turn?

children.note: Trichoderma protects roots through several actions at once, which is why pathogens rarely become resistant to it.
Trichoderma coils around the threads of disease fungi and dissolves their walls with enzymes such as chitinases and glucanases, then feeds on them.

manas.q: What is mycoparasitism?

children.note: It grows quickly and occupies root surfaces and organic matter first, taking space and nutrients that pathogens need to infect the root.
It releases antifungal compounds, including volatile and non-volatile metabolites, that slow or stop the growth of nearby pathogens.
When it colonises roots, the plant's own defence system is primed, so the whole plant responds faster to later attacks.

manas.q: Besides attacking pathogens directly, how does Trichoderma protect the whole plant?

children.note: Many strains improve root branching and help nutrient uptake, partly by solubilising some nutrients and producing growth-promoting substances. Effects vary with strain and soil.
It works best against soil-borne fungal diseases and is preventive. It is not a remedy for leaf diseases or for crops already badly infected.
Seedlings rot at the soil line or fail to emerge in nurseries. Trichoderma in seed treatment and nursery media is a standard preventive measure.

manas.q: Which nursery disease is Trichoderma seed treatment mainly used to prevent?

children.note: Roots become brown or black and decay, causing poor growth and plant death; common in pulses, cotton, vegetables and many other crops.
Fungal wilts block the water-conducting tissue, so plants droop and die even when the soil is moist.
Main targets are soil fungi and fungus-like organisms that attack roots and stem bases.
Causes vascular wilts in tomato, banana, chickpea, pigeonpea and others. Trichoderma reduces infection pressure but cannot cure an already wilted plant.
Causes damping off, root rot and sheath blight; often seen as brown sunken lesions at the stem base.
A water mould (oomycete) favoured by waterlogged soil; a major cause of seedling damping off.

manas.q: Which damping-off pathogen is favoured by waterlogged soil?

children.note: Sclerotium rolfsii causes collar rot and southern blight; it forms white fan-like growth and mustard-seed-like sclerotia at the stem base.
Recognising soil-borne disease early helps decide when Trichoderma should be part of the plan.
Pre-emergence damping off shows as gaps in rows; post-emergence shows thin, water-soaked stems that topple over.

manas.q: What does post-emergence damping off look like?

children.note: Pulled-up plants show decayed, soft or dry rotted roots with few fine roots.
Splitting the lower stem of a Fusarium-wilted plant shows brown discoloured vessels; wilting often starts on one side.

manas.q: What do you see when you split the stem of a Fusarium-wilted plant?

children.note: White cottony growth with small round brown sclerotia at the stem base points to Sclerotium collar rot.
Fewer gaps in nursery beds, healthier white roots, less wilting over seasons; green Trichoderma growth may be visible on enriched manure.
Use it before disease appears: on seed, in the nursery, in manure and in the soil. Follow the label dose; values below are common extension recommendations.
Seed is coated with the powder, often about 4 g per kg seed with a little water or sticker, dried in shade and sown the same day.

manas.q: What is a common Trichoderma seed-treatment dose?

children.note: Mix the product into nursery soil or cocopeat and drench seedling trays to protect young seedlings from damping off.
Dip transplant roots in a Trichoderma suspension for a short time before planting to give them a protective coat.
Mix the product with well-decomposed, moist farmyard manure, cover with a wet sack in shade, turn occasionally and apply after about 1–2 weeks when green growth appears.

manas.q: How do farmers multiply Trichoderma on the farm before soil application?

children.note: Enriched FYM is broadcast in furrows or around plants at sowing or planting, and repeated in perennial crops at the root zone.
A water suspension is poured around the stem base of seedlings or established plants to protect the root zone.
It needs moist soil and organic matter to establish. Dry soil, direct sun on the product and very low organic matter reduce its survival.
Generic product types; check registration, CFU count and expiry date on every pack. No single form suits every farm.
The most common form in India: spores mixed with talc or another inert carrier. Easy for seed treatment and FYM enrichment.
Liquid and wettable-powder forms suit drip, drenching and spraying, and often have longer shelf life than plain talc products.
Strength is given in colony-forming units per gram. Indian registration guidelines for talc Trichoderma require at least about 2 × 10⁶ CFU per gram.

manas.q: What does CFU on a Trichoderma label mean?

children.note: Talc products typically keep about 6 months; keep in a cool, dry, shaded place and use before the expiry date.

manas.q: How should Trichoderma products be stored?

children.note: Some products combine Trichoderma with bacterial agents such as Pseudomonas; check that the label lists each organism and its count.
Living fungus: many chemical fungicides kill it, while organic manures help it.
Systemic fungicides such as carbendazim and other benzimidazoles are particularly harmful. Do not mix it in the same seed treatment or tank.

manas.q: Why should Trichoderma not be mixed with carbendazim?

children.note: If a chemical fungicide must be used, apply it separately and leave a gap before using Trichoderma, as advised by local extension.
Compost, FYM and neem cake give it food and help it build up in soil.
It is commonly used alongside Rhizobium, Azotobacter or PSB; apply on the same seed in sequence, with the biofungicide first, as advised.
Treat it as one part of integrated disease management, not a guarantee.
Best results come when it is applied before or at sowing. It cannot revive plants already wilted or rotted.
Repeated use with organic matter builds up suppressive soil; benefits are often clearer after several seasons.
Soil moisture, temperature, organic matter, strain and product quality all change how well it works.
Common errors that waste money or kill the product.
Using it in the same seed treatment as a chemical fungicide can kill the spores and leave seed unprotected.
Without moisture and organic matter it struggles to establish; always apply to moist soil, ideally with manure.
It mainly protects against soil-borne fungi. Leaf spots, viruses and insect pests need other measures.
Spores die with age and heat; an old pack may contain few living units.
Biocontrol agents are regulated as biopesticides, not fertilizers.
Trichoderma products are registered as biopesticides under the Insecticides Act with the Central Insecticides Board; buy registered products.

manas.q: Under which Indian authority are Trichoderma products registered?

children.note: In Kenya, Trichoderma products must be registered by the Pest Control Products Board; KEPHIS handles plant health and imported microbes.
Trichoderma is widely accepted in organic production; check certifier rules for the specific product.

nodeData.note: Three groups of beneficial bacteria used as biological disease control agents. They protect plants by producing antibiotics, competing for iron and space, and switching on the plant's own defences.

children.note: A common root-colonising bacterium used as a biocontrol and growth-promoting agent in many crops.
A free-living, rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacterium that lives on root surfaces (rhizobacterium). It glows yellow-green under UV light on certain media.

manas.q: Is Pseudomonas fluorescens a fungus or a bacterium?

children.note: It makes iron-binding molecules that grab scarce iron in the root zone, starving pathogens of iron.

manas.q: How do siderophores help suppress pathogens?

children.note: Strains produce antimicrobial compounds such as 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol, phenazines and pyoluteorin that inhibit fungi and bacteria.
Root colonisation primes defences throughout the plant, so leaves can resist some diseases even though the bacteria stay at the roots.

manas.q: What is induced systemic resistance (ISR)?

children.note: It can improve root growth and nutrient uptake, partly through plant hormones and phosphate solubilisation in some strains.
Used against a range of fungal and some bacterial diseases, mostly as a preventive.
In India it is widely recommended for rice, used as seed treatment, seedling dip and foliar spray to reduce blast and sheath blight.
Can lower bacterial wilt in solanaceous crops when combined with resistant varieties, rotation and hygiene, but it is not a stand-alone cure.
Protects roots against Pythium, Rhizoctonia and Fusarium in nurseries and field crops.
As a non-spore-former it is more sensitive to heat and drying than Bacillus, so storage and shade matter more.
Spore-forming bacteria that make tough, long-lasting biocontrol products.
A Gram-positive, spore-forming soil bacterium used against many fungal leaf and root diseases.

manas.q: Why do Bacillus products usually have a longer shelf life?

children.note: A close relative of B. subtilis, known for strong antifungal lipopeptides and root colonisation.
Many strains formerly sold as B. amyloliquefaciens are now classified as B. velezensis; it is a strong producer of antimicrobial compounds.

manas.q: What is the newer name for many biocontrol strains once called B. amyloliquefaciens?

children.note: Bacillus forms resting spores that survive heat, drying and long storage, which gives products longer shelf life.
They produce compounds such as surfactin, iturin and fengycin that damage fungal cell membranes.

manas.q: Name the lipopeptide antibiotics made by Bacillus.

children.note: Used as seed treatment and drench for root diseases and as foliar spray against some leaf and fruit fungi; also induces plant resistance.
Filamentous soil bacteria (actinomycetes) and the source of many medical antibiotics.
Gram-positive bacteria that grow as branching threads like fungi and give soil its earthy smell (geosmin).

manas.q: What gives freshly dug soil its earthy smell?

children.note: Produces antifungal and antibacterial compounds, enzymes that break down fungal walls, and colonises roots to compete with pathogens.
Biocontrol species such as S. griseoviridis and S. lydicus are used against root rots and damping off, mainly in vegetables and nurseries.
Know the symptoms these agents are used to prevent.
Spindle-shaped spots with grey centres and brown margins on leaves; neck blast causes empty, broken panicles.

manas.q: What do rice blast leaf spots look like?

children.note: Oval greenish-grey lesions on sheaths near the waterline that enlarge and merge.
Whole plants wilt suddenly while still green; a cut stem in clear water releases milky bacterial streams.

manas.q: What simple test points to bacterial wilt?

children.note: Seedlings collapse at the soil line, and older plants have brown, decayed roots and stunted growth.
Common extension practices; always follow the label dose and timing.
Coat seed with the powder and a little water just before sowing; Pseudomonas is often used at about 10 g per kg seed.

manas.q: What is a common Pseudomonas seed-treatment dose?

children.note: Soak transplant roots, for example rice seedlings, in a suspension for about 30 minutes before planting.
Mix the product with well-decomposed FYM or compost and apply to moist soil at sowing or planting.
Liquid products can be poured around the stem base or given through drip for root-zone diseases.
Used for some leaf diseases such as rice blast; spray in the cool evening so UV and heat do less damage.
Generic forms; no brand names. Check registration number, CFU count and expiry.
Carrier-based powder common in India; easy for seed treatment and FYM enrichment, typically with about 6 months' shelf life.
Suited to drip, drench and spray; usually longer shelf life than powders when stored correctly.
Bacillus products are often sold as wettable powders or granules because their spores remain stable.
Strength is stated as CFU per gram or ml; the registration sets a minimum for each organism. Choose fresh packs with clearly stated counts.
Keep cool, dry and out of sunlight; never leave packs in a hot vehicle or store.
Living bacteria must be kept away from chemicals that kill them.
Copper fungicides and bactericidal antibiotics such as streptomycin can kill these bacteria; do not tank-mix.

manas.q: Which chemicals kill bacterial biocontrol agents in a tank mix?

children.note: Bacteria often tolerate some fungicides better than Trichoderma does, but compatibility varies; check the label or separate applications.
Pseudomonas and Trichoderma are often used together or in consortium products to cover more pathogens.
FYM, compost and neem cake improve survival and spread in soil.
Where these agents are most often used.
Pseudomonas is a common part of rice disease management in India, from seed to transplanting and spray.
Seed treatment and tray drenches protect tomato, chilli, brinjal and cabbage seedlings from damping off.
Applied with FYM to the root zone to help against soil-borne wilts and rots, alongside clean planting material.
Seed treatment helps protect against root rot and wilt in early growth stages.
Use them as part of integrated disease management.
They reduce disease pressure when applied early; they do not cure plants that are already badly infected.
Strain, product quality, soil, weather and timing all affect how well they work in the field.
Common errors with bacterial biocontrol.
These agents work best preventively; spraying only after heavy infection gives poor results.

children.topic: Myth: Bacillus is always the same
children.note: Effect depends strongly on the strain; two Bacillus products can perform very differently.
UV and heat kill Pseudomonas quickly; mix in shade and use the suspension the same day.
These products are regulated as biopesticides.
Pseudomonas fluorescens and Bacillus products are registered as biopesticides with the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee.
Biocontrol products must be registered by the Pest Control Products Board before sale; use only registered products.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body registers biopesticides?

children.note: Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.

children.note: How it suppresses root diseases.
Trichoderma, Pseudomonas and Bacillus production.

Why these soil actinomycetes help gardens.

Overview of the bacterium, its biocontrol compounds and uses.
Overview of B. subtilis biology, spores and agricultural use.
Overview of the genus and its antibiotic production.

nodeData.note: Living fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes that make insect pests and nematodes sick. They act more slowly and more selectively than chemical pesticides and work best as part of integrated pest management (IPM).

children.note: Microbial biopesticides are products whose active ingredient is a living microorganism (or its toxin) that infects or poisons a pest.
Fungi (Beauveria, Metarhizium, Lecanicillium, Purpureocillium), bacteria (Bacillus thuringiensis), viruses (NPV) and insect-killing nematodes.

manas.q: What are the four main groups of microbial biopesticides?

children.note: They are safe for people, livestock and most natural enemies, leave little or no harmful residue, and help manage pests that have become resistant to chemicals.
They kill slowly (days, not hours), need the right humidity, temperature and timing, and are living products that die if stored or mixed badly.
Best results come when they are applied early, when pest numbers are still low, and repeated. They are weak as a last-minute rescue in a heavy outbreak.

manas.q: Are microbial biopesticides best as early prevention or emergency rescue?

children.note: An insect-killing fungus found naturally in soils worldwide. It causes white muscardine disease in a wide range of insects.
A soil fungus (entomopathogen) that does not need to be eaten: its spores infect insects by touching their skin.

manas.q: Does Beauveria need to be eaten by the insect to infect it?

children.note: Spores stick to the insect cuticle, germinate and push through it with enzymes and pressure. The fungus grows inside the body, uses up its contents and releases toxins; the insect dies in several days.
Caterpillars, beetles and weevils (including banana weevil and coffee berry borer), stem borers, whiteflies, thrips, aphids and termites.
Dead insects become stiff and mummified, then are covered by a white, powdery or cottony fungal coat, first at the joints. This is proof the fungus is working.

manas.q: What colour is the fungal growth on insects killed by Beauveria?

children.note: Background on the fungus, its host range and its use in biological control.
An insect-killing soil fungus that causes green muscardine disease. It is especially useful against soil-dwelling pests.
A soil fungus that infects insects through the skin, like Beauveria. Related species (e.g. Metarhizium acridum) are used against locusts and grasshoppers.
White grubs, termites, root weevils, rhinoceros beetle in coconut, sugarcane and soil pests, plus locusts and grasshoppers (special strains).
Killed insects harden and get a white growth that turns olive to dark green as the fungus produces spores.

manas.q: What colour do insects killed by Metarhizium turn?

children.note: Mix the product with well-decomposed compost or FYM and place it in the root zone or planting hole, then keep the soil moist, so the fungus establishes where grubs live.
Background on Metarhizium species and their biology.
A fungus best known for attacking sap-sucking insects. Older literature calls it Verticillium lecanii.
An entomopathogenic fungus now named Lecanicillium (several species); the old name Verticillium lecanii is still printed on many labels.

manas.q: What is the older name of Lecanicillium lecanii?

children.note: Soft-bodied sucking pests: whiteflies, aphids, mealybugs, scales and thrips, mostly in greenhouses and humid crops.
Infected insects are covered with a white to cream fuzzy growth; scales and whitefly nymphs get a white halo around them.
It needs long periods of high humidity, so it suits greenhouses, dense canopies and rainy seasons better than dry open fields.
Taxonomy and biocontrol use of Lecanicillium.
A soil fungus (formerly Paecilomyces lilacinus) used against plant-parasitic nematodes, especially root-knot nematodes.
A common soil fungus that parasitises nematode eggs and females. Its old name, Paecilomyces lilacinus, is still widely used.

manas.q: Which pest group does Purpureocillium (Paecilomyces) lilacinus control?

children.note: Fungal threads grow into nematode egg masses and eggs, killing the developing juveniles, which lowers the next generation in the soil.
Roots with knots or galls, stunted, wilting plants in patches despite water, and yellowing: signs of root-knot nematode in tomato, vegetables, banana and pulses.
Mix with compost or neem cake, apply to nursery beds, planting holes or the root zone, or use as a seedling root dip; keep soil moist and repeat in later seasons.
Taxonomy and nematode-control use of the fungus.
A soil bacterium whose protein crystals poison caterpillars and some other insect larvae once eaten.
A spore-forming bacterium. When it forms spores it also makes crystal (Cry) proteins that are toxic to specific insect groups.
The larva must eat it. The gut's alkaline juice dissolves the crystal, the activated toxin punches holes in the gut wall, and the insect stops feeding within hours and dies in a few days.

manas.q: Why must Bt be eaten to work?

children.note: Subspecies kurstaki and aizawai target caterpillars (moths); israelensis targets mosquito and blackfly larvae; tenebrionis targets some beetle larvae.

manas.q: Which Bt subspecies is used against mosquito larvae?

children.note: Larvae stop feeding, become sluggish, darken and shrivel; damage stops quickly even though dead larvae may appear only after 2–3 days.
Spray young larvae, cover the leaves they feed on, and spray in the evening because sunlight (UV) breaks down the toxin.

Nuclear polyhedrosis viruses (baculoviruses) that infect caterpillars of one or a few closely related species.
